claim: Under natural conditions, the visual system often sees a given input repeatedly.
source: Under natural conditions, the visual system often sees a given input repeatedly.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural visual experience, drawing from established knowledge about visual processing.

claim: Stimulus repetition provides an opportunity to optimize processing of the repeated stimuli.
source: This provides an opportunity to optimize processing of the repeated stimuli.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on inference about the functional significance of repeated stimuli.

claim: Stimulus repetition has been shown to strongly modulate neuronal-gamma band synchronization.
source: Stimulus repetition has been shown to strongly modulate neuronal-gamma band synchronization, yet crucial questions remained open.
evidence: This statement references prior research findings without specific citations in this sentence, drawing on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Gamma decreases across approximately 10 repetitions and then increases across further repetitions in human subjects.
source: Here we used magnetoencephalography in 30 human subjects and find that gamma decreases across ≈10 repetitions and then increases across further repetitions, revealing plastic changes of the activated neuronal circuits.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MEG data collected in this study.

claim: Gamma increases induced by one stimulus did not affect responses to other stimuli.
source: Crucially, increases induced by one stimulus did not affect responses to other stimuli, demonstrating stimulus specificity.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental data showing stimulus-specific effects.

claim: Changes in gamma partially persisted when the inducing stimulus was repeated after 25 minutes of intervening stimuli.
source: Changes partially persisted when the inducing stimulus was repeated after 25 minutes of intervening stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from the experimental design comparing block A and block A2.

claim: Gamma changes were strongest in early visual cortex.
source: They were strongest in early visual cortex and increased interareal feedforward influences.
evidence: This is based on source-localized MEG data showing spatial distribution of effects.

claim: Gamma changes increased interareal feedforward influences.
source: They were strongest in early visual cortex and increased interareal feedforward influences.
evidence: This is based on Granger causality analysis of the MEG data.

claim: Early visual cortex gamma synchronization enables adaptive neuronal processing of recurring stimuli.
source: Our results suggest that early visual cortex gamma synchronization enables adaptive neuronal processing of recurring stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, presented as a suggestion.

claim: The reported changes might be due to an interaction of oscillatory dynamics with established synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
source: These and previously reported changes might be due to an interaction of oscillatory dynamics with established synaptic plasticity mechanisms.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed phenomena.

claim: Organisms rarely encounter random and temporally independent visual inputs in natural environments.
source: While moving through natural environments, organisms rarely encounter random and temporally independent visual inputs.
evidence: This is a general statement about natural visual statistics based on established knowledge.

claim: A specific environment comes with its own distribution of probable edge orientations, object categories, and visual image statistics.
source: A specific environment comes with its own distribution of probable edge orientations, object categories, and visual image statistics in general (Torralba and Oliva, 2003), and as organisms spend extended periods in the same environment, their visual input is likely to be autocorrelated (Dong and Atick, 1995) and self-repeating (Wilming et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Visual input is likely to be autocorrelated as organisms spend extended periods in the same environment.
source: A specific environment comes with its own distribution of probable edge orientations, object categories, and visual image statistics in general (Torralba and Oliva, 2003), and as organisms spend extended periods in the same environment, their visual input is likely to be autocorrelated (Dong and Atick, 1995) and self-repeating (Wilming et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Dong and Atick, 1995.

claim: Visual input is likely to be self-repeating as organisms spend extended periods in the same environment.
source: A specific environment comes with its own distribution of probable edge orientations, object categories, and visual image statistics in general (Torralba and Oliva, 2003), and as organisms spend extended periods in the same environment, their visual input is likely to be autocorrelated (Dong and Atick, 1995) and self-repeating (Wilming et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wilming et al., 2013.

claim: Stimulus repetition leads to a reduction of firing rates in stimulus-driven neurons in visual areas.
source: Stimulus repetition has been shown to lead to a reduction of firing rates in stimulus-driven neurons (Desimone, 1996; Li et al., 1993) and a decreased hemodynamic response (Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Stern et al., 1996) in visual areas, a phenomenon generally called repetition suppression.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Desimone, 1996; Li et al., 1993).

claim: Stimulus repetition leads to a decreased hemodynamic response in visual areas.
source: Stimulus repetition has been shown to lead to a reduction of firing rates in stimulus-driven neurons (Desimone, 1996; Li et al., 1993) and a decreased hemodynamic response (Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Stern et al., 1996) in visual areas, a phenomenon generally called repetition suppression.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research (Grill-Spector et al., 2006; Stern et al., 1996).

claim: The decrease of neuronal activity with repetition does not lead to decreases in detection performance.
source: Importantly, this decrease of neuronal activity does not lead to decreases in detection performance.
evidence: This statement is based on prior research findings in the field.

claim: Detection performance generally stays stable or even improves over stimulus repetitions.
source: Instead, detection performance generally stays stable or even improves over stimulus repetitions (Fiorentini and Berardi, 1980; Grill-Spector et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Repetition suppression might specifically target neurons coding for redundant, already predicted, information.
source: Potentially, repetition suppression might specifically target neurons coding for redundant, already predicted, information (Auksztulewicz and Friston, 2016).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility supported by citation.

claim: Neurons most responsive to repeated input might be exempted from repetition suppression.
source: Alternatively, behavior might rely primarily on the neurons most responsive to the repeated input, which might be exempted from repetition suppression (Desimone, 1996; Homann et al., 2017) or might even undergo repetition enhancement (Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility supported by citations.

claim: Neurons most responsive to repeated input might undergo repetition enhancement.
source: Alternatively, behavior might rely primarily on the neurons most responsive to the repeated input, which might be exempted from repetition suppression (Desimone, 1996; Homann et al., 2017) or might even undergo repetition enhancement (Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility supported by citation to Lim et al., 2015.

claim: Non-suppressed neurons might fire more synchronously, compensating for decreased firing rates via increased temporal overlap between action potentials.
source: Consistent with the latter, a further possibility is that the remaining, non-suppressed neurons fire more synchronously, effectively compensating for decreased firing rates via increased temporal overlap between action potentials (Gotts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical possibility supported by citation.

claim: In area V1, an increase in synchronous neuronal firing and oscillatory power in the gamma band has been reported with stimulus repetition.
source: In area V1, such an increase in synchronous neuronal firing and oscillatory power in the gamma band has been reported (Brunet et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Gamma-band power in V1 increased with the logarithm of the number of repetitions.
source: Specifically, gamma-band power in the local field potential increased with the logarithm of the number of repetitions, accompanied by increased V1–V4 coherence and gamma spike-field locking in V4.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Brunet et al., 2014.

claim: Stimulus repetition increased V1-V4 coherence.
source: Specifically, gamma-band power in the local field potential increased with the logarithm of the number of repetitions, accompanied by increased V1–V4 coherence and gamma spike-field locking in V4.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Brunet et al., 2014.

claim: Stimulus repetition increased gamma spike-field locking in V4.
source: Specifically, gamma-band power in the local field potential increased with the logarithm of the number of repetitions, accompanied by increased V1–V4 coherence and gamma spike-field locking in V4.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Brunet et al., 2014.

claim: The repetition-related gamma enhancement effect is present in humans.
source: We found that the repetition-related gamma enhancement effect is clearly present in humans, is stimulus specific, and persists over time and deadaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the MEG study with 30 human participants.

claim: The repetition-related gamma enhancement effect is stimulus specific.
source: We found that the repetition-related gamma enhancement effect is clearly present in humans, is stimulus specific, and persists over time and deadaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experimental design with different stimulus orientations.

claim: The repetition-related gamma enhancement effect persists over time and deadaptation.
source: We found that the repetition-related gamma enhancement effect is clearly present in humans, is stimulus specific, and persists over time and deadaptation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing block A and block A2.

claim: Changes in reaction times and accuracy were not correlated to changes in gamma power over subjects.
source: Changes in reaction times and accuracy were not correlated to changes in gamma power over subjects (see below).
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis between behavioral and neural measures.

claim: Grating stimuli produced robust responses in visual areas.
source: As expected, grating stimuli produced robust responses in visual areas: Dipoles in V1/V2 showed a clear visual ERF and a stimulus-driven gamma-band response (Figure 2a–d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is a finding from MEG source localization analysis.

claim: Dipoles in V1/V2 showed a clear visual ERF and a stimulus-driven gamma-band response.
source: As expected, grating stimuli produced robust responses in visual areas: Dipoles in V1/V2 showed a clear visual ERF and a stimulus-driven gamma-band response (Figure 2a–d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: This is a finding from MEG source localization analysis shown in figures.

claim: The gamma-band response was strongest in areas V1 and V2 and extended into temporal and parietal lobes.
source: The gamma-band response was strongest in areas V1 and V2 and extended into temporal and parietal lobes (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is a finding from spatial analysis of MEG data shown in Figure 2e.

claim: A stimulus-driven decrease in source-localized alpha and beta power could be seen in temporal/parietal and parietal/frontal areas, respectively.
source: Furthermore, a stimulus-driven decrease in source-localized alpha and beta power could be seen in temporal/parietal and parietal/frontal areas, respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is a finding from spectral analysis of MEG data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: When the visual stimulus was switched at the beginning of a new block, the pattern of early decrease and subsequent increase repeated.
source: When the visual stimulus was switched at the beginning of a new block, this pattern of early decrease and subsequent increase repeated.
evidence: This is a finding from analysis across blocks with different stimuli.

claim: Repetition-related gamma increases were specific to the repeated stimulus because block boundaries were only constituted by switches in stimulus orientation.
source: This demonstrates that these repetition-related gamma increases were specific to the repeated stimulus because block boundaries were only constituted by switches in stimulus orientation.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design and observed pattern of results.

claim: Both the early decrease in gamma power and the gamma-power increase source-localized to visual cortical areas and were strongest in V1, V2, V3, and V4.
source: Both the early decrease in gamma power and the gamma-power increase source-localized to visual cortical areas and were strongest in V1, V2, V3, and V4 (Figure 3e,f; for sensor-level analysis, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: This is a finding from spatial analysis of MEG source-localized data shown in figures.

claim: The repetition-related increase was specific to the gamma band.
source: The repetition-related increase was specific to the gamma band (Figure 3d,g).
evidence: This is a finding from spectral analysis shown in figures.

claim: The gamma-power increase could not have been driven by changes in microsaccade rate.
source: These observations together show that the gamma-power increase could not have been driven by changes in MS rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the microsaccade analysis results.

claim: Granger causality between cortical areas in the gamma band is stronger in the anatomically defined feedforward direction.
source: Previous studies in macaques and humans found that Granger causality (GC) between cortical areas in the gamma band is stronger in the anatomically defined feedforward direction, whereas GC in the alpha-beta band is stronger in the feedback direction (Bastos et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Granger causality between cortical areas in the alpha-beta band is stronger in the feedback direction.
source: Previous studies in macaques and humans found that Granger causality (GC) between cortical areas in the gamma band is stronger in the anatomically defined feedforward direction, whereas GC in the alpha-beta band is stronger in the feedback direction (Bastos et al., 2015; Michalareas et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The present dataset found a similar pattern of Granger causality results to Michalareas et al., 2016.
source: We repeated the core analysis of Michalareas et al., 2016 for the present dataset and found a similar pattern of results (Figure 5a,b, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from replication analysis shown in figures.

claim: Significant Granger causality changes with stimulus repetition were strongly clustered in the gamma band.
source: Across all area pairs, significant GC changes with stimulus repetition were strongly clustered in the gamma band, while no significant changes in the alpha-beta band were found (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from spectral analysis of GC changes shown in Figure 5c.

claim: No significant Granger causality changes in the alpha-beta band were found with stimulus repetition.
source: Across all area pairs, significant GC changes with stimulus repetition were strongly clustered in the gamma band, while no significant changes in the alpha-beta band were found (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is a finding from spectral analysis of GC changes shown in Figure 5c.

claim: With stimulus repetition, feedforward gamma Granger causality increased from V1 to V2/V3/V4.
source: With stimulus repetition, across all between-area pairs, feedforward gamma GC increased from V1 to V2/V3/V4, and from V3/V3AB/V4 to several areas further up the dorsal and ventral streams (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This is a finding from directional GC analysis shown in Figure 5d,e.

claim: With stimulus repetition, feedforward gamma Granger causality increased from V3/V3AB/V4 to several areas further up the dorsal and ventral streams.
source: With stimulus repetition, across all between-area pairs, feedforward gamma GC increased from V1 to V2/V3/V4, and from V3/V3AB/V4 to several areas further up the dorsal and ventral streams (Figure 5d,e).
evidence: This is a finding from directional GC analysis shown in Figure 5d,e.

claim: Feedback Granger causality onto areas V1-V4 increased with stimulus repetition.
source: Feedback GC onto areas V1–V4 also increased.
evidence: This is a finding from directional GC analysis.

claim: The changes in gamma Granger causality were not purely driven by changes in the signal-to-noise ratio of the gamma band.
source: This demonstrates that the changes in gamma GC were not purely driven by changes in the signal-to-noise ratio of the gamma band.
evidence: This is an inference from the control analysis results.

claim: Repeated presentations of a visual stimulus induced gamma-band activity in early and intermediate visual areas that decreased over the initial 10 repetitions and subsequently increased over further repetitions.
source: In summary, repeated presentations of a visual stimulus induced gamma-band activity in early and intermediate visual areas that decreased over the initial 10 repetitions and subsequently increased over further repetitions.
evidence: This is a summary of the primary findings from the study.

claim: When stimuli were switched, the pattern of early gamma decrease and subsequent increase repeated.
source: Crucially, when stimuli were switched, this pattern repeated.
evidence: This is a summary of findings demonstrating stimulus specificity.

claim: The changes in neuronal circuits that underlie the observed gamma-power increase are specific to the repeated stimulus.
source: This strongly suggests that the changes in the neuronal circuits that underlie the observed gamma-power increase are specific to the repeated stimulus and do not equally affect the processing of other stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference from the stimulus-specific pattern of results.

claim: Gamma peak frequency increased over repetitions and did not show distinct changes for the first few repetitions.
source: Gamma peak frequency increased over repetitions and did not show distinct changes for the first few repetitions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about gamma frequency changes.

claim: The stimulus-specific increases in gamma power and frequency with repetitions showed a stimulus-specific memory effect.
source: The stimulus-specific increases in gamma power and frequency with repetitions showed a stimulus-specific memory effect, in the sense that some enhancement persisted over 25 minutes of stimulation with different stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about persistence of effects.

claim: The repetition-driven network changes are at least partially persistent.
source: This suggests that the repetition-driven network changes are at least partially persistent.
evidence: This is an inference from the persistence findings.

claim: Gamma-band Granger causality increased with stimulus repetitions, especially from early visual areas in the anatomically defined feedforward direction.
source: Furthermore, gamma-band Granger causality increased with stimulus repetitions, especially from early visual areas in the anatomically defined feedforward direction.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about directional connectivity changes.

claim: The magnitude of early ERF components decreased linearly with stimulus repetitions.
source: In addition, the magnitude of early ERF components decreased linearly with stimulus repetitions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about ERF changes.

claim: The repetition-related changes occurred over two different timescales, potentially indicative of two distinct but co-occurring processes.
source: The repetition-related changes occurred over two different timescales, potentially indicative of two distinct but co-occurring processes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal pattern of results.

claim: Over the first 10 stimulus repetitions, gamma power and pupil constriction decreased, and the slopes of their decreases were correlated across subjects.
source: Over the first 10 stimulus repetitions, gamma power and pupil constriction decreased, and the slopes of their decreases were correlated across subjects.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about early changes in gamma and pupil measures.

claim: Over the remaining repetitions, gamma power increased continuously, while pupil constriction remained at the lower level.
source: Over the remaining repetitions, gamma power increased continuously, while pupil constriction remained at the lower level.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about late changes in gamma and pupil measures.

claim: The pattern of changes is consistent with the superposition of an exponential decay with a slow and steady increase.
source: This pattern of changes is consistent with the superposition of an exponential decay, seen in gamma power and pupil constriction, with a slow and steady increase, seen in gamma power.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal dynamics of the results.

claim: Gamma peak frequency steadily increased over all repetitions of a given stimulus.
source: In support of this scenario, two other parameters of neuronal activity showed such changes over all repetitions of a given stimulus: Gamma peak frequency steadily increased, and the magnitude of an early ERF component steadily decreased.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supporting the two-process interpretation.

claim: The magnitude of an early ERF component steadily decreased over all repetitions of a given stimulus.
source: In support of this scenario, two other parameters of neuronal activity showed such changes over all repetitions of a given stimulus: Gamma peak frequency steadily increased, and the magnitude of an early ERF component steadily decreased.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supporting the two-process interpretation.

claim: There are remarkable similarities between gamma-band activities and their repetition-related changes measurable in both non-human primates and humans.
source: By extending research on gamma repetition enhancement from non-human primate local field potential recordings to human source-localized MEG, we could show remarkable similarities between gamma-band activities and their repetition-related changes, measurable in both species and recording techniques – see the companion paper (Peter et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparative statement supported by reference to a companion paper.

claim: Existing animal studies are limited to two to four subjects and thereby to an inference on those samples.
source: Notably, the existing studies with animals are limited to two to four subjects and thereby to an inference on those samples, whereas the present MEG study recorded from 30 subjects and thereby allowed an inference on the population.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of inference in prior animal studies versus the current study.

claim: The present MEG study recorded from 30 subjects and thereby allowed an inference on the population.
source: Notably, the existing studies with animals are limited to two to four subjects and thereby to an inference on those samples, whereas the present MEG study recorded from 30 subjects and thereby allowed an inference on the population.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope of inference in the current study.

claim: Careful head stabilization and exclusion of participants with excessive head movements enables a spatial resolution between 0.45 mm and 7 mm in MEG source localization.
source: Nevertheless, careful head stabilization and exclusion of participants with excessive head movements, as implemented in this study, enables a spatial resolution between 0.45 mm and 7 mm (Nasiotis et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Granger causality does not necessarily imply the existence of true neuronal interactions between time series, but merely implies predictability of one time series by another.
source: When analyzing Granger causality, it is important to stress that GC does not necessarily imply the existence of true neuronal interactions between time series, but merely implies predictability of one time series by another (Kispersky et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a methodological caveat supported by citation.

claim: Common noise and field spread in signals analyzed using Granger causality can lead to spurious inferred connectivity.
source: Additionally, common noise and field spread in signals analyzed using GC can lead to spurious inferred connectivity, which can, however, be mostly alleviated using time-reversal testing, as used in this study (Haufe et al., 2012; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological caveat and solution supported by citations.

claim: Time-reversal testing can mostly alleviate spurious inferred connectivity from common noise and field spread.
source: Additionally, common noise and field spread in signals analyzed using GC can lead to spurious inferred connectivity, which can, however, be mostly alleviated using time-reversal testing, as used in this study (Haufe et al., 2012; Vinck et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by citations.

claim: The first trial of each block showed strong induced gamma power, followed by a decrease over the following nine trials.
source: In our recordings, the first trial of each block showed strong induced gamma power, followed by a decrease over the following nine trials.
evidence: This is a description of the observed pattern in the data.

claim: Stimulus switches were unexpected to subjects.
source: As subjects had not been informed about the different orientations, their blocked order, or the block length, stimulus switches were unexpected.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and subject knowledge.

claim: Grating stimuli were mostly novel to subjects.
source: Furthermore, as grating stimuli were not shown during training and subjects were recruited from the general public, grating stimuli were mostly novel.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design and subject experience.

claim: Unexpected and novel stimuli have been shown to induce stronger neuronal responses in early visual cortex.
source: Unexpected and novel stimuli have been shown to induce stronger neuronal responses in early visual cortex: In an fMRI paradigm, subjects showed hemodynamic response increases in V1 when a presented grating had a different orientation to the one expected by the subjects (Kok et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: In an fMRI paradigm, subjects showed hemodynamic response increases in V1 when a presented grating had a different orientation to the one expected.
source: Unexpected and novel stimuli have been shown to induce stronger neuronal responses in early visual cortex: In an fMRI paradigm, subjects showed hemodynamic response increases in V1 when a presented grating had a different orientation to the one expected by the subjects (Kok et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Kok et al., 2016.

claim: In an MEG study, the occipital cortex showed stronger activation when the expected stimulus sequence was violated or when stimuli were presented that subjects were not familiar with.
source: In an MEG study, in which subjects learned that presented visual stimuli followed a specific stimulus sequence, the occipital cortex showed stronger activation when the expected stimulus sequence was violated or when stimuli were presented that the subjects were not familiar with (Manahova et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Manahova et al., 2018.

claim: Pupil diameter has been linked to arousal in several studies.
source: Pupil diameter has been linked to arousal in several studies (de Gee et al., 2017; Peinkhofer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The pupillary light reflex can be influenced by arousal, attention, and stimulus novelty.
source: Paradigms including luminance increases, as used here, induce pupil constrictions, referred to as the pupillary light reflex, which can also be influenced by arousal, attention, and stimulus novelty (Binda et al., 2013; Naber et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Pupil constrictions were strong on initial stimulus presentation, decreasing over the first ten repetitions and remaining low for further repetitions.
source: In our data, pupil constrictions were strong on initial stimulus presentation, decreasing over the first ten repetitions and remaining low for further repetitions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about pupil constriction patterns.

claim: Gamma power showed correlated dynamics with pupil constriction for the initial 10 presentations of a given stimulus.
source: Gamma power showed correlated dynamics for the initial 10 presentations of a given stimulus, but showed increases for further repetitions.
evidence: This is a summary of findings about the relationship between gamma and pupil measures.

claim: Stimulus novelty leads to strong gamma and pupil responses for the initial presentation of a stimulus and rapid decline thereafter.
source: This is consistent with a scenario in which stimulus novelty leads to strong gamma and pupil responses for the initial presentation of a stimulus and the rapid decline thereafter, and other mechanisms lead to the steady increase in gamma for later repetitions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed pattern of results.

claim: Other mechanisms lead to the steady increase in gamma for later repetitions.
source: This is consistent with a scenario in which stimulus novelty leads to strong gamma and pupil responses for the initial presentation of a stimulus and the rapid decline thereafter, and other mechanisms lead to the steady increase in gamma for later repetitions.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about mechanisms.

claim: The late increases brought gamma power approximately back to the level of the first few repetitions in a block.
source: In the present study, the late increases brought gamma power approximately back to the level of the first few repetitions in a block.
evidence: This is an observation about the magnitude of gamma changes.

claim: Data obtained with invasive recordings in macaque monkeys show that the gamma-power decrease during early trials can be strongly exceeded by the increase during later trials.
source: However, data obtained with invasive recordings in macaque monkeys show that the gamma-power decrease during early trials can be strongly exceeded by the increase during later trials (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In macaque areas V1 and V4, the across-trial repetition of stimuli induced strong firing rate decreases over the first few repetitions as well as smaller firing rate decreases over further repetitions.
source: In macaque areas V1 and V4, the across-trial repetition of stimuli induced strong firing rate decreases over the first few repetitions as well as smaller firing rate decreases over further repetitions (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In macaque V4, firing rate decreases have been reported within single trials, between the first and immediately following second presentation of a given stimulus.
source: In macaque V4, firing rate decreases have also been reported within single trials, between the first and immediately following second presentation of a given stimulus (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: In mouse V1, within-session repetition-driven decrease in neuronal activity occurred as a sparsification of the neuronal response.
source: In mouse V1, such a within-session repetition-driven decrease in neuronal activity, measured using calcium imaging, occurred as a sparsification of the neuronal response: While most measured neurons decreased their activity with repetitions, a small set of strongly driven neurons stayed continually active even after repetitions (Homann et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Homann et al., 2017.

claim: In macaque V2, firing rate responses were smaller for familiar than for novel images from 100 ms post-stimulus onset.
source: In macaque V2, firing rate responses were smaller for familiar than for novel images from 100 ms post-stimulus onset (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2018.

claim: When macaques were trained to identify grating orientations over several months, tuning curves of V1 neurons responsive to orientations close to the trained orientation steepened at the trained orientation.
source: When macaques were trained to identify grating orientations over several months, tuning curves of V1 neurons responsive to orientations close to the trained orientation steepened at the trained orientation (Schoups et al., 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Schoups et al., 2001.

claim: In large populations of neurons recorded in macaque IT, putative excitatory neurons showed higher selectivity to images the monkeys had been familiarized with over months compared to novel images.
source: In large populations of neurons recorded in macaque IT, putative excitatory neurons showed higher selectivity to images the monkeys had been familiarized with over months compared to novel images (Lim et al., 2015; Woloszyn and Sheinberg, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In anesthetized macaque V1, when the neuronal response to an oriented grating stimulus was adapted by presentation for 40 s, a subsequent display of the same orientation induced weaker gamma power, whereas other orientations induced stronger gamma power.
source: In anesthetized macaque V1, when the neuronal response to an oriented grating stimulus was adapted by presentation for 40 s (plus additional top-up presentations), a subsequent display of the same orientation induced weaker gamma power, whereas other orientations induced stronger gamma power (Jia et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Jia et al., 2011.

claim: Decreases in broadband gamma power but increases in broadband gamma spike-field locking with one-shot adaptation have been recorded in awake macaque V4.
source: In addition, decreases in broadband gamma power but increases in broadband gamma spike-field locking with one-shot adaptation have also been recorded in awake macaque V4, and have been hypothesized to be driven by synaptic depression (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: In human MEG and fMRI, the second presentation of familiar visual stimuli induced weaker gamma-band power and weaker hemodynamic responses in early visual areas than the first one.
source: In human MEG and fMRI, the second presentation of familiar visual stimuli induced weaker gamma-band power and weaker hemodynamic responses in early visual areas than the first one (Friese et al., 2012a; Friese et al., 2012b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A study of macaque V1 and V4 activity found that LFP gamma power and frequency in both areas, and their coherence, increased with the logarithm of repetition number.
source: A study of macaque V1 and V4 activity (Brunet et al., 2014), using up to 600 repetitions of few similar grating stimuli, found that LFP gamma power and frequency in both areas, and their coherence, increased with the logarithm of repetition number.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brunet et al., 2014.

claim: Stimulus repetition affected gamma spike-field locking in V4: For putative interneurons, it increased, and for putative pyramidal cells, there was a positive relationship between their stimulus drivenness and the slope of repetition-related changes in locking.
source: Furthermore, stimulus repetition also affected gamma spike-field locking in V4: For putative interneurons, it increased, and for putative pyramidal cells, there was a positive relationship between their stimulus drivenness and the slope of repetition-related changes in locking.
evidence: This statement refers to findings from Brunet et al., 2014.

claim: The companion paper investigated repetition-related gamma increases in macaque V1 and found that they are also specific to the repeated stimulus, have some persistence, and generalize to natural stimuli.
source: The companion paper to the one presented here investigated repetition-related gamma increases in macaque V1 and found that they are also specific to the repeated stimulus, have some persistence, and generalize to natural stimuli (Peter et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to the companion paper.

claim: In the locust antennal lobe, odor repetition decreased firing of excitatory neurons to a limited set of reliably firing neurons and increased power and spike-field locking in the dominant odor-driven LFP oscillation (the beta band) in a stimulus-specific fashion.
source: In the locust antennal lobe, odor repetition decreased firing of excitatory neurons to a limited set of reliably firing neurons and increased power and spike-field locking in the dominant odor-driven LFP oscillation (the beta band) in a stimulus-specific fashion (Bazhenov et al., 2005; Stopfer and Laurent, 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the rat, odor-driven gamma-band oscillations in the olfactory bulb and the orbitofrontal cortex increased with odor repetition during task learning.
source: In the rat, odor-driven gamma-band oscillations in the olfactory bulb and the orbitofrontal cortex also increased with odor repetition during task learning (Beshel et al., 2007; van Wingerden et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Oscillatory neuronal activity can interact with Hebbian spike-timing-dependent plasticity.
source: Oscillatory neuronal activity can interact with Hebbian spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP).
evidence: This is a statement about known mechanisms in neuroscience.

claim: Interaction between oscillatory activity and STDP can lead to changes in synaptic weights between excitatory neurons that enhance their temporal synchronization and establish excitatory cell assemblies.
source: This can, for example, lead to changes in synaptic weights between excitatory neurons (E-E) that enhance their temporal synchronization and establish excitatory cell assemblies (Arthur et al., 2005; Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007; Suri and Sejnowski, 2002) as well as shorten oscillatory cycles (Börgers, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Interaction between oscillatory activity and STDP can shorten oscillatory cycles.
source: This can, for example, lead to changes in synaptic weights between excitatory neurons (E-E) that enhance their temporal synchronization and establish excitatory cell assemblies (Arthur et al., 2005; Cassenaer and Laurent, 2007; Suri and Sejnowski, 2002) as well as shorten oscillatory cycles (Börgers, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Börgers, 2017.

claim: When visual stimulation induces gamma-band activity in awake primate V1, the resulting gamma cycles contain systematic sequences where the better a neuron is driven by a given stimulus, the earlier it spikes in the gamma cycle.
source: When visual stimulation induces gamma-band activity in awake primate V1 (Brunet et al., 2015; Jia et al., 2011; Kreiter and Singer, 1992; Uran et al., 2020), the resulting gamma cycles contain systematic sequences: The better a neuron is driven by a given stimulus, the earlier it spikes in the gamma cycle (Fries et al., 2007; Havenith et al., 2011; König et al., 1995; Vinck et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The gamma cycle contains a characteristic sequence of excitation and inhibition.
source: This is likely due to the fact that the gamma cycle contains a characteristic sequence of excitation and inhibition (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Vinck et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Excitation triggers inhibition during the gamma cycle, and when inhibition decays, the most driven neurons are the first to overcome inhibition and spike.
source: Excitation triggers inhibition, and when inhibition decays, the most driven neurons are the first to overcome inhibition and spike.
evidence: This is a description of gamma cycle dynamics based on established knowledge.

claim: Spiking of the most driven neurons leads to a new rise in inhibition, and only sufficiently driven neurons spike before the rising inhibition prevents the least driven neurons from spiking at all.
source: Their spiking leads to a new rise in inhibition, and only sufficiently driven neurons spike before the rising inhibition prevents the least driven neurons from spiking at all (de Almeida et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to de Almeida et al., 2009.

claim: On average, the most driven excitatory neurons spike first, followed by spiking of local inhibitory neurons, while less driven excitatory neurons spike during and after the inhibitory neurons.
source: Thus, on average, the most driven excitatory neurons (Estrong) spike first, followed by spiking of local inhibitory neurons (Ilocal), while less driven excitatory neurons (Eweak) spike during and after the inhibitory neurons, if at all.
evidence: This is a summary of the spike timing sequence during gamma cycles.

claim: If two neurons spike for some time with a systematic temporal relationship, this can lead to changes in their mutual synaptic inputs, a phenomenon referred to as spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP).
source: If two neurons spike for some time with a systematic temporal relationship, this can lead to changes in their mutual synaptic inputs, a phenomenon referred to as spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) (Caporale and Dan, 2008; Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The precise pattern of synaptic strengthening and weakening as a function of relative spike timing varies across neuron types and brain areas.
source: The precise pattern of synaptic strengthening and weakening as a function of the relative spike timing varies across neuron types and brain areas (Hennequin et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Hennequin et al., 2017.

claim: Hebbian STDP has been described for synapses of excitatory neurons onto inhibitory neurons in rat visual cortex.
source: This pattern has, e.g., been described for synapses of excitatory neurons onto inhibitory neurons in rat visual cortex (Huang et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Huang et al., 2013.

claim: Hebbian STDP, together with the Estrong-Ilocal-Eweak sequence during gamma cycles, would lead to a strengthening of the synapses from Estrong to Ilocal, and to a weakening of the synapses from Eweak to Ilocal.
source: This Hebbian STDP, together with the abovementioned Estrong-Ilocal-Eweak sequence during gamma cycles, would lead to a strengthening of the synapses from Estrong to Ilocal, and to a weakening of the synapses from Eweak to Ilocal.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on combining known mechanisms.

claim: A Hebbian-type I-to-E STDP has been found in rat entorhinal cortex.
source: Yet, a Hebbian-type I-to-E STDP has been found in rat entorhinal cortex (Haas et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Haas et al., 2006.

claim: Hebbian I-to-E STDP together with the gamma-related Estrong-Ilocal-Eweak sequence could lead to strengthening of synapses from Ilocal to Eweak and weakening of synapses from Ilocal to Estrong.
source: Together with the gamma-related Estrong-Ilocal-Eweak sequence, this could lead to strengthening of synapses from Ilocal to Eweak and weakening of synapses from Ilocal to Estrong.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on combining known mechanisms.

claim: The activation of Estrong neurons during repeated presentation of a given stimulus would increase the impact of Estrong onto Ilocal neurons through the interplay between gamma cycle and STDP.
source: Through this interplay between the gamma cycle and STDP, the activation of Estrong neurons during the repeated presentation of a given stimulus would increase the impact of Estrong onto Ilocal neurons.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the mechanism.

claim: Estrong spiking would trigger Ilocal spiking with more efficiency and shorter latency, leading to stronger and earlier Ilocal spiking, and thereby more gamma-locked Ilocal spiking.
source: Estrong spiking would trigger Ilocal spiking with more efficiency and shorter latency, leading to stronger and earlier Ilocal spiking, and thereby more gamma-locked Ilocal spiking.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the mechanism.

claim: The proposed mechanism could explain the observed shorter gamma cycles and overall stronger gamma power.
source: This could explain the observed shorter gamma cycles (i.e., higher gamma frequency) and overall stronger gamma power measured here and in macaques (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2020), and the increasing gamma locking of inhibitory neurons (Brunet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for the observed findings.

claim: The proposed mechanism could explain the increasing gamma locking of inhibitory neurons.
source: This could explain the observed shorter gamma cycles (i.e., higher gamma frequency) and overall stronger gamma power measured here and in macaques (Brunet et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2020), and the increasing gamma locking of inhibitory neurons (Brunet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for findings from prior research.

claim: Stronger and more synchronized bouts of Ilocal spiking would enhance the impact of Ilocal neurons onto Eweak neurons.
source: At the same time, these stronger and more synchronized bouts of Ilocal spiking would enhance the impact of Ilocal neurons onto Eweak neurons.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the mechanism.

claim: The inhibition of Eweak neurons would be further enhanced by the strengthened Ilocal-to-Eweak synapses.
source: Additionally, the inhibition of Eweak neurons would be further enhanced by the strengthened Ilocal-to-Eweak synapses.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction about the mechanism.

claim: The proposed mechanism could lead to maintained firing of Estrong together with reduced firing of Eweak neurons, implementing a winner-take-all mechanism that sharpens the population firing rate representation.
source: In sum, this could lead to maintained firing of Estrong together with reduced firing of Eweak neurons, and thereby explain overall reduced firing rates and implement a winner-take-all mechanism that sharpens the population firing rate representation (de Almeida et al., 2009; Homann et al., 2017; Lim et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation for observed phenomena, supported by citations.

claim: The overall increase in gamma strength and the stronger focusing of Estrong spiking during the early gamma cycle would likely enhance the impact of the local Estrong neurons onto their postsynaptic target neurons in other areas.
source: Beyond these local effects, the overall increase in gamma strength and the stronger focusing of Estrong spiking during the early gamma cycle would likely enhance the impact of the local Estrong neurons onto their postsynaptic target neurons in other areas (Salinas and Sejnowski, 2000).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction supported by citation.

claim: The proposed mechanism is consistent with the observed repetition-related enhancement of V1-V4 gamma coherence.
source: This is consistent with the observed repetition-related enhancement of V1–V4 gamma coherence (Brunet et al., 2014) and of feedforward gamma GC (this study).
evidence: This is a statement about consistency between the proposed mechanism and observed findings.

claim: The proposed mechanism is consistent with the observed repetition-related enhancement of feedforward gamma Granger causality.
source: This is consistent with the observed repetition-related enhancement of V1–V4 gamma coherence (Brunet et al., 2014) and of feedforward gamma GC (this study).
evidence: This is a statement about consistency between the proposed mechanism and observed findings.

claim: The sharpened neuronal population response might be communicated more efficiently through increased synchronization.
source: Thereby, the sharpened neuronal population response might be communicated more efficiently (Lewis et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citation.

claim: Increased synchronization would compensate for overall lower firing rates, allowing the visual system to keep or improve behavioral performance with less neuronal activity.
source: Increased synchronization would compensate for overall lower firing rates, thereby allowing the visual system to keep or improve behavioral performance with less neuronal activity (Gotts et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a theoretical statement supported by citation.

claim: The proposed changes should be specific to the activated cell assembly, extend over time and be robust to deadaptation.
source: Such changes should be specific to the activated cell assembly, extend over time and be robust to deadaptation, as shown in this study.
evidence: This is a prediction from the proposed mechanism that is consistent with the study findings.

claim: 30 participants successfully completed the experiment.
source: Participants were recruited from the general public until 30 had successfully completed the experiment.
evidence: This is a statement about the study sample.

claim: Twenty of the 30 participants were male.
source: Twenty of the 30 participants were male.
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the study sample.

claim: Participants were of an average age of 22 years (range: 19-28 years).
source: They were of an average age of 22 years (range: 19–28 years), had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, were free of metal implants, did not use medication during the study period except for contraceptives, and had never been diagnosed with any neurological or psychiatric disorder.
evidence: This is a demographic characteristic of the study sample.

claim: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the medical faculty of the Goethe University Frankfurt.
source: The study was approved by the ethics committee of the medical faculty of the Goethe University Frankfurt (Resolution E 36/18).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Visual stimuli were back-projected onto a screen 53 cm away from subjects' eyes using a Propixx projector.
source: Visual stimuli were back-projected onto a screen 53 cm away from their eyes using a Propixx projector (Resolution: 960*520 px, 1440 Hz refresh rate).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The stimulus was a centrally presented square wave grating with a diameter of 22.9 degrees of visual angle and a spatial frequency of 4 cycles/dva.
source: The stimulus was a centrally presented square wave grating with anti-aliasing (i.e., slightly rounded edges), with a diameter of 22.9 degrees of visual angle (dva), a spatial frequency of 4 cycles/dva, and one of the following orientations: 22.5 deg, 67.5 deg, 121.5 deg, 175.5 deg.
evidence: This is a description of the visual stimulus properties.

claim: A total of 600 trials were recorded for each subject, composed of 5 blocks of 120 trials.
source: For each subject, a total of 600 trials were recorded, composed of 5 blocks of 120 trials.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Blocks were labeled A, B, C, D, A2, with A2 constituting a repetition of block A.
source: Blocks were labeled A, B, C, D, A2, with the letters randomly assigned (per participant) to one of the four orientations, and A2 constituting a repetition of block A.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: There was no break, change or instruction of any kind between blocks.
source: Note that trials proceeded seamlessly across block boundaries, i.e. there was no break, change or instruction of any kind between blocks, and subjects were instructed to disregard stimulus orientation.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The whole experiment lasted 45 min on average.
source: The whole experiment lasted 45 min on average, giving a time interval of approximately 27 min between the end of block A and the beginning of block A2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timing.

claim: There was a time interval of approximately 27 min between the end of block A and the beginning of block A2.
source: The whole experiment lasted 45 min on average, giving a time interval of approximately 27 min between the end of block A and the beginning of block A2.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental timing.

claim: Data were recorded using an MEG system comprising 275 axial gradiometers.
source: Data were recorded using an MEG system (CTF Systems) comprising 275 axial gradiometers, low-pass filtered (300 Hz), and digitized (1200 Hz).
evidence: This is a description of the recording equipment.

claim: Subjects were trained before the experiment to avoid eye blinks during the baseline and stimulation period.
source: Subjects were trained before the experiment to avoid eye blinks during the baseline and stimulation period and to instead blink during each inter-trial interval.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Blinks occurred in merely 3.9% of all analyzed trials.
source: Therefore, blinks occurred in merely 3.9% of all analyzed trials.
evidence: This is a result of the blink training procedure.

claim: Head drift >5 mm away from the initial head position was considered excessive.
source: Head drift >5 mm away from the initial head position was considered excessive.
evidence: This is a description of the data quality criterion.

claim: Nine subjects were excluded due to excessive head drift, falling asleep, hardware malfunctions, or similar problems.
source: Excessive head drift, falling asleep, hardware malfunctions, or similar problems resulted in immediate abortion of the recording session and exclusion of the respective subject from the study. Any break or interruption to fix those problems would have interfered with the repetition protocol. In total, this exclusion applied to nine subjects, which were not counted toward the 30 subjects reported here.
evidence: This is a description of the exclusion criteria and number of excluded subjects.

claim: Artifact-free parts of epochs were used for analyses if they contained data for the full respective analysis window lengths, which was the case for 76% of trials.
source: Artifact-free parts of the respective epochs were used for the analyses described below if they contained data for the full respective analysis window lengths, which was the case for 76% of trials.
evidence: This is a description of the data inclusion rate.

claim: Subject-specific gamma peak was found for all subjects.
source: This procedure found a subject-specific gamma peak for all subjects.
evidence: This is a result of the frequency analysis procedure.

claim: All selected dipoles for V1/V2 analysis were located in areas V1 or V2.
source: All selected dipoles were located in areas V1 or V2.
evidence: This is a result of the source localization procedure shown in Figure 2a.
